entities.summary: John Chojeński (1486–1538) was a Polish bureaucrat and church leader who played a pivotal role in the Catholic Reformation in Poland. He was a key figure in the establishment of the Polish Protestant Church and was appointed as the bishop of Kraków in 1534. Chojeński's influence extended beyond Poland's borders, as he collaborated with Protestant reformers in Germany and was influenced by the ideas of Martin Luther. The Polish Protestant Church he established had a lasting impact on the country's religious landscape, and its legacy can still be seen in the modern-day Polish Catholic Church. Chojeński's efforts also had a lasting impact on the Catholic Church, as he was instrumental in the Council of Trent, a major ecumenical council that shaped the Church's doctrine and practices. Chojeński's story is a testament to the complex and often fraught relationship between Catholicism and Protestantism in Poland during the 16th century. His legacy is a reminder of the power of religious conviction and the enduring impact of historical events on the course of human history.

He was a key figure in the establishment of the Polish Reformation, which sought to reform the Catholic Church in Poland. The movement was influenced by the ideas of Martin Luther and other Protestant reformers. Chojeński's contributions to the Polish Reformation helped shape the country's religious landscape for centuries to come. He was also a prominent figure in the Polish nobility, serving as a diplomat and military commander. Chojeński's legacy extends beyond his religious accomplishments, as he was also a patron of the arts and education. He was particularly close to the Polish king, Sigismund I the Old, who supported his religious and cultural endeavors. Chojeński's life and work serve as a testament to the complex and often fraught relationships between church and state in early modern Poland.
